content: The initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) among infants living with HIV remains suboptimal, despite the universal recommendation for treatment initiation in this population. Globally, ART coverage among children lags significantly behind that of adults, with only 32% of eligible children receiving treatment compared to 40% of adults as of 2014. Diagnosing and retaining children exposed to or living with HIV in care is uniquely challenging due to their dependence on caregivers. Loss to follow-up is particularly high, especially among children in HIV care who are not receiving ART. The 2013 WHO antiretroviral (ARV) guidelines aligned ART eligibility criteria for children older than five years with those for adults, recommending treatment for those with WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 disease or CD4 counts at or below 500 cells/mm³. For children younger than five years, ART was recommended regardless of clinical or immunological status. Among children aged one to five years, priority was given to those younger than two years with WHO stage 3 or 4 disease, CD4 percentages below 25%, or CD4 counts below 750 cells/mm³. For infants younger than one year, a strong recommendation was made to initiate treatment regardless of clinical or immunological conditions. The guidelines acknowledged the challenges of treating infants in the first two weeks of life due to limited treatment options with established safe and effective dosing, compounded by high rates of prematurity and low birth weight in lowand middle-income countries. ART initiation is recommended for all children living with HIV, regardless of WHO clinical stage or CD4 cell count. Infants diagnosed within the first year of life should receive immediate treatment, supported by moderate-quality evidence. For children aged one to less than ten years, ART initiation is conditionally recommended due to limited evidence, but this approach is expected to provide significant programmatic advantages, particularly in settings with limited access to immunological testing and low ART coverage. Early ART initiation has been shown to slightly but significantly reduce mortality compared to waiting for CD4 counts to fall below 500 cells/mm³. Early treatment also promotes better growth responses and may mitigate the negative effects of HIV on growth, pubertal development, and nervous system development. Additionally, earlier ART initiation may enhance immune recovery. Studies have demonstrated that children with greater immunosuppression at baseline do not recover to normal CD4 levels even after five years of ART, whereas those starting ART at higher CD4 levels normalize within a year. Early ART initiation is also likely to reduce chronic immune activation induced by HIV, potentially limiting the onset of chronic lung disease and cardiovascular disease. Programmatic experience suggests that children receiving ART have better retention in care compared to those not receiving ART. Simplifying ART initiation criteria has been associated with increased ART coverage and more rapid treatment initiation. However, earlier ART initiation may pose risks, including short-term side effects that could lead to suboptimal adherence, treatment failure, and the emergence of drug resistance. Long-term side effects and chronic disease may increase morbidity and affect quality of life in adulthood. Despite these potential harms, the clinical and programmatic benefits of earlier ART initiation are likely to outweigh the risks. Expanding ART to all children living with HIV is expected to increase equity and be well-accepted by communities. Psychosocial support for parents and caregivers, particularly regarding disclosure, is critical to facilitating treatment initiation and improving adherence. Implementing this recommendation is feasible, representing a relatively small additional burden on health systems. However, increased numbers of children receiving ART may place higher demands on supply chain systems and provider workloads. National programs have demonstrated the feasibility of treating all children with HIV but highlight the importance of secure commodity supplies, adequate health worker training, and sustainable resources. Research gaps remain regarding the effects of earlier ART on retention, adherence, and potential drug resistance among children with less advanced disease. Optimal service delivery models to ensure rapid identification and ART initiation among infants and children need further investigation. Strategies to provide integrated care packages to reduce overall child mortality are also needed.
